claim: Electrical junctions are widespread within the mammalian CNS.
source: Electrical junctions are widespread within the mammalian CNS.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the prevalence of electrical junctions in the mammalian central nervous system.

claim: The role of electrical junctions in organizing neuronal ensemble activity remains incompletely understood.
source: Yet, their role in organizing neuronal ensemble activity remains incompletely understood.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: Rat TIDA cells discharge in highly stereotyped, robust, synchronized slow oscillations.
source: rat TIDA cells discharge in highly stereotyped, robust, synchronized slow oscillations
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including electrophysiological recordings and calcium imaging.

claim: Mouse TIDA oscillations are faster, flexible and show substantial cell-to-cell variability.
source: whereas mouse oscillations are faster, flexible and show substantial cell-to-cell variability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse TIDA neuron recordings.

claim: Rat TIDA neurons have strong TIDA-TIDA gap junction coupling.
source: We show that these distinct operational modes are explained by the presence of strong TIDA-TIDA gap junction coupling in the rat
evidence: This is supported by paired recordings showing electrical coupling and Cx36 immunostaining data.

claim: Mouse TIDA neurons completely lack gap junction coupling.
source: and its complete absence in the mouse.
evidence: This is supported by paired recordings showing no electrical coupling and absence of Cx36 immunostaining in mouse TIDA neurons.

claim: Both rat and mouse species encompass a similar heterogeneous range of intrinsic resonance frequencies.
source: Both species, however, encompass a similar heterogeneous range of intrinsic resonance frequencies, suggesting similar network building blocks.
evidence: This is supported by ZAP function experiments measuring preferred frequencies in both species.

claim: Gap junctions select and impose the slow network rhythm in rat TIDA neurons.
source: We demonstrate that gap junctions select and impose the slow network rhythm.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that postjunctional resonance frequency matches oscillation frequency in electrically coupled rat TIDA neurons.

claim: Electrical junctions determine oscillation frequency in neuronal networks.
source: These data identify a role for electrical junctions in determining oscillation frequency
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental comparison of rat and mouse TIDA networks.

claim: Related species can rely on distinct network strategies to accomplish adaptive control of hormone release.
source: and show how related species can rely on distinct network strategies to accomplish adaptive control of hormone release.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed differences in electrical coupling between rat and mouse TIDA neurons.

claim: Neuronal gap junctions were once surmised to be exclusive to invertebrate species and/or early development.
source: While once surmised to be exclusive to invertebrate species and/or early development, steadily accumulating evidence has established that electrical junctions formed by gap junctions are both common and consequential within many populations in the adult, mammalian CNS (see Connors and Long, 2004).
evidence: This is a historical statement about past scientific understanding, supported by citation.

claim: Electrical junctions formed by gap junctions are both common and consequential within many populations in the adult, mammalian CNS.
source: While once surmised to be exclusive to invertebrate species and/or early development, steadily accumulating evidence has established that electrical junctions formed by gap junctions are both common and consequential within many populations in the adult, mammalian CNS (see Connors and Long, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Gap junctions mediate ultra-fast, subthreshold, bidirectional cell-cell communication.
source: By mediating ultra-fast, subthreshold, bidirectional (albeit not always symmetrical) cell-cell communication
evidence: This is established knowledge about the properties of gap junctions.

claim: Gap junctions have been implicated in the synchronization of neuronal activity.
source: gap junctions have been implicated most obviously in the synchronization (e.g. Christie et al., 1989; Beierlein et al., 2000; Dugué et al., 2009) of neuronal activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gap junctions can interact with parallel chemical synaptic transmission between neurons.
source: The particular kinetics of electrical junctions further allow them to for example interact with the parallel chemical synaptic transmission between neurons (e.g. Llinas et al., 1974; Mathy et al., 2014; see Pereda, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gap junctions can spread intracellular messengers between cells.
source: and spread intracellular messengers between cells (Tsien and Weingart, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The presence of gap junctions changes the computational rules within circuits.
source: The presence of gap junctions changes the computational rules within circuits.
evidence: This is a general statement about the functional impact of gap junctions, based on established knowledge.

claim: Oscillations are intrinsic to brain networks throughout the neuraxis.
source: Oscillations are intrinsic to brain networks throughout the neuraxis (see Buzsáki and Watson, 2012), appearing in wide, but stereotyped, frequency spectra.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Shifts in network frequency have been proposed to correspond to changes in the information carried across neuronal transmission.
source: Shifts in network frequency have been proposed to correspond to changes in the information carried across neuronal transmission (see Singer and Gray, 1995)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A switch in period can denote the conversion of a physiological oscillation into a pathological rhythm.
source: and a switch in period can denote the conversion of a physiological oscillation into a pathological rhythm (Kostopoulos et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: There is little experimental data addressing how gap junctions influence or set the specific frequency of a network oscillation.
source: While the issue of whether (and if so, how) gap junctions influence, or even set, the specific frequency of a network oscillation has been the subject of a limited number of elegant modeling and theoretical studies (Kepler et al., 1990; Meunier, 1992; Pedersen et al., 2005), there is little experimental data addressing this important issue.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a gap in experimental evidence, with citation to theoretical studies.

claim: Pharmacological tools for studying gap junctions are compromised by poor specificity.
source: This dearth of information can in no small measure be ascribed to limitations in the available methodological repertoire: pharmacological tools are compromised by poor specificity (e.g. Beaumont and Maccaferri, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Genetically manipulated animals often exhibit incomplete loss-of-function of gap junctions.
source: whereas genetically manipulated animals, although informative in several aspects, often exhibit incomplete loss-of-function (De Zeeuw et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TIDA neurons oscillate between depolarized UP and hyperpolarized DOWN states.
source: Here, studying the neuroendocrine tuberoinfundibular dopamine (TIDA) neurons, which oscillate between depolarized UP and hyperpolarized DOWN states (Lyons et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Tuberoinfundibular dopamine neurons in the hypothalamic dorsomedial arcuate nucleus of rats exhibit a slow, robust, highly rhythmic, synchronized network oscillation in vitro.
source: Tuberoinfundibular dopamine neurons in the hypothalamic dorsomedial arcuate nucleus (dmArc) of rats exhibit a slow, robust, highly rhythmic, synchronized network oscillation in vitro (Lyons et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Reports on mouse TIDA neurons describe notably irregular fast phasic firing.
source: Reports on mouse TIDA neurons, however, describe notably irregular fast phasic firing (Brown et al., 2012; Romanò et al., 2013; Zhang and van den Pol, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dichotomy across analogous rodent circuits are rare in the literature.
source: Such dichotomy across analogous rodent circuits are rare in the literature.
evidence: This is a statement about the rarity of such observations in scientific literature.

claim: Male rat TIDA cells exhibit a stereotyped slow oscillation at 0.15 ± 0.01 Hz.
source: Male rat TIDA cells identified by their location in the dmArc (Figure 1A–B) and characteristic electrical properties (Lyons et al., 2010), exhibited a stereotyped slow (0.15 ± 0.01 Hz; n = 29, Figure 1C,G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Rat TIDA neurons exhibit a highly regular oscillation with coefficient of variation for frequency of 1.99 ± 0.69%.
source: and highly regular (coefficient of variation (CV) for frequency = 1.99 ± 0.69%; n = 8 slices; Figure 1H) oscillation
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Mouse TIDA neurons exhibit significantly faster oscillations (0.39 ± 0.05 Hz) than rat TIDA neurons.
source: these oscillations were significantly faster (0.39 ± 0.05 Hz; n = 18–29 per group, Figure 1F,G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Mouse TIDA neurons are less rhythmic than rat TIDA neurons.
source: less rhythmic (Figure 1H)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing autocorrelograms.

claim: Mouse TIDA neurons show a wide range of frequencies within the same slice with CV = 41.48 ± 6.19%.
source: of a wide range of frequencies within the same slice (Figure 1G; CV = 41.48 ± 6.19%; n = 8 slices)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Mouse TIDA oscillation nadir is more depolarized (-51.2 ± 0.9 mV) than rat (-66.0 ± 1.1 mV).
source: and more depolarized (mouse oscillation nadir −51.2 ± 0.9 mV vs. rat −66.0 ± 1.1 mV; n = 18 per group).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: An oscillatory current is seen in voltage clamp mode only in rat TIDA neurons.
source: An oscillatory current was seen in voltage clamp mode only in rat TIDA neurons (Figure 1C,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from voltage clamp recordings.

claim: Rat TIDA oscillation frequency is insensitive to hyperpolarization.
source: Furthermore, rat TIDA oscillation frequency was insensitive to hyperpolarization (Figure 1I–K)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no change in frequency with hyperpolarizing current.

claim: Mouse TIDA cells progressively decrease their frequency in response to negative current until it collapses below ca. −80 mV.
source: whereas mouse TIDA cells progressively decreased their frequency in response to negative current until it collapsed to a stable membrane potential below ca. −80 mV (Figure 1L–N).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing frequency changes with hyperpolarization.

claim: Rat TIDA oscillations maintain their frequency when challenged with ZAP current.
source: Rat TIDA oscillations maintained their frequency when challenged with ZAP I (Figure 1O,P).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ZAP current injection experiments.

claim: Application of ZAP current to mouse TIDA neurons results in full entrainment of the cells' rhythm.
source: In contrast, application of the same protocol to mouse TIDA neurons resulted in a full entrainment of the cells' rhythm (Figure 1Q,R).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ZAP current injection experiments.

claim: The cross-correlation coefficient between recorded cell frequency and current command is significantly lower in rat (0.61 ± 0.03) compared to mouse (0.87 ± 0.01).
source: The cross-correlation coefficient of the frequency of the recorded cell and the current command was thus significantly lower in rat (0.61 ± 0.03; n = 10) compared to mouse (0.87 ± 0.01; n = 10; Figure 1S,T)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ZAP current injection experiments.

claim: The rat TIDA oscillation is robust against perturbation, in contrast to the mouse.
source: demonstrating the rat TIDA oscillation is robust against perturbation, in contrast to the mouse.
evidence: This is inferred from the cross-correlation coefficient data.

claim: Paired recordings from rat TIDA neurons reveal pronounced phase-locked synchronicity between cells.
source: Paired recordings from rat TIDA neurons revealed pronounced phase-locked synchronicity between cells (n = 63 pairs; Figure 3A,B; see also Lyons et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from paired electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Mouse TIDA cells are asynchronous.
source: in contrast to mouse TIDA cells, which were asynchronous (n = 40 pairs; Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from paired electrophysiological recordings.

claim: A cluster of rat TIDA cells in the dmArc exhibit spontaneous, slow synchronized Ca2+ oscillations at 0.15 ± 0.01 Hz.
source: Using Oregon green-BAPTA in rat slices, a cluster of cells in the dmArc exhibited spontaneous, slow synchronized Ca2+ oscillations (0.15 ± 0.01 Hz; Figure 3E,F,I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-photon calcium imaging.

claim: Fluctuations in membrane potential and Ca2+ activity are strongly correlated in mouse TIDA neurons.
source: Simultaneous whole-cell and Ca2+ recordings in mouse TIDA neurons revealed strongly correlated fluctuations in membrane potential and Ca2+ activity, indicating that they reflect the same underlying cellular phenomena (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from simultaneous electrophysiology and calcium imaging.

claim: Mouse TIDA cells exhibit asynchronous, fast Ca2+ oscillations (0.40 ± 0.05 Hz) with large variability.
source: In agreement with electrophysiology, cells exhibited asynchronous, fast (0.40 ± 0.05 Hz; Figure 3G–I) oscillation frequencies, with large variability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging.

claim: The species differences found at the single-cell level are paralleled in the rat and mouse TIDA network.
source: These data show that the species differences found at the single-cell level are paralleled in the rat and mouse TIDA network.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of single-cell and network-level data.

claim: Rat and mouse TIDA neurons have similar electrophysiological signatures including a prominent A-like K+ current, anomalous inward rectification and slow after hyperpolarization.
source: In whole-cell recordings, rat and mouse TIDA neurons were found to have similar electrophysiological signatures, such as a prominent A-like K+ current, anomalous inward rectification and slow after hyperpolarization (Lyons et al., 2010; Zhang and van den Pol, 2015) - Figure 4A,B,E,F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings and citations to previous studies.

claim: Rat and mouse TIDA neurons have partly different amplitude of electrophysiological properties.
source: albeit of partly different amplitude (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Oscillations in both rat and mouse TIDA neurons are abolished in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX).
source: In both species, oscillations were abolished in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX; Figure 4L)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from TTX application experiments.

claim: TIDA neuron oscillations depend on the persistent Na+ current for phasic firing.
source: suggesting a similar dependence on the persistent Na+ current for phasic firing (Lyons et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the TTX abolition of oscillations and supported by citation.

claim: Oscillations persist in both rat and mouse TIDA neurons during blockade of fast ionotropic glutamate and GABA transmission.
source: Importantly, in both rats and mice, oscillations persisted during blockade of fast ionotropic glutamate and GABA transmission (Figure 4M)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pharmacological blockade experiments.

claim: Chemical synapses are not required for the expression of rhythmic behavior in TIDA neurons.
source: suggesting that chemical synapses are not required for the expression of rhythmic behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistence of oscillations during blockade of fast synaptic transmission.

claim: Earlier work has suggested the existence of gap junctions in rat TIDA neurons.
source: Earlier work (Lyons et al., 2010) has suggested the existence of gap junctions in rat TIDA neurons, but direct evidence for electrical coupling has been lacking.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Direct evidence for electrical coupling in rat TIDA neurons has been lacking prior to this study.
source: Earlier work (Lyons et al., 2010) has suggested the existence of gap junctions in rat TIDA neurons, but direct evidence for electrical coupling has been lacking.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a gap in previous evidence.

claim: Electrical coupling is found in 51% of rat TIDA neuron pairs with a high coupling coefficient of 0.18 ± 0.02.
source: Recordings of sub-threshold voltage transfer (Bennett, 1966) in rat TIDA neuron pairs revealed electrical coupling in 51% (n = 32/63) of pairs with a high coupling coefficient (CC = 0.18 ± 0.02; Figure 5A–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from paired electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Electrical coupling in rat TIDA neurons is in the highest range reported in the mammalian brain.
source: This electrical coupling is in the highest range reported in the mammalian brain (Curti et al., 2012), with single pairs reaching as high as 0.48 CC.
evidence: This is a comparison to previously reported values, supported by citation.

claim: Electrical coupling in rat TIDA neurons is typically asymmetrical with strongest:weakest ratio of 1.52 ± 0.17.
source: Coupling was typically asymmetrical (strongest: weakest ratio, 1.52 ± 0.17; n = 16; Figure 5F, top).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from paired electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Mouse TIDA neuron pairs show no evidence of electrical coupling and/or synchrony.
source: In notable contrast, mouse TIDA neuron pairs (n = 40) showed no evidence of electrical coupling and/or synchrony (Figure 5G–L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from paired electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Punctate Cx36 immunoreactivity is distributed along rat TH-ir dendrites and somata.
source: Punctate Cx36 immunoreactivity was found distributed along rat (n = 4 animals), but not mouse (n = 7 animals), TH-ir dendrites and somata (Figure 5M,N)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry.

claim: Cx36 immunoreactivity is not found in mouse TIDA neurons.
source: Punctate Cx36 immunoreactivity was found distributed along rat (n = 4 animals), but not mouse (n = 7 animals), TH-ir dendrites and somata (Figure 5M,N)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry.

claim: The antibody readily detects Cx36 in other mouse brain populations.
source: even though the antibody readily detects Cx36 in other mouse brain populations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry in other brain regions.

claim: There is an absolute species difference in TIDA gap junction connectivity between rat and mouse.
source: These data identify an absolute species difference in TIDA gap junction connectivity.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined electrophysiological and immunohistochemical data.

claim: The lack of electrical coupling in mouse TIDA neurons explains their higher input resistance.
source: The lack of electrical coupling in the mouse TIDA neurons can also explain their higher input resistance (Figure 4C,D,G,H; cf. De Zeeuw et al., 2003)
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between electrical coupling and input resistance, supported by citation.

claim: The lack of electrical coupling in mouse TIDA neurons explains their more fragile oscillation dynamics.
source: and their more fragile oscillation dynamics (Figure 1C,F,I–T).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of oscillation robustness between species.

claim: The rat-mouse species difference in electrical coupling offers an experimental model to address functional aspects of gap junctions in rhythmically active systems.
source: Importantly, the rodent TIDA species difference in electrical coupling offers an experimental model to address functional aspects of the role of gap junctions in rhythmically active systems, in a manner that avoids the poor pharmacological specificity of gap junction-blocking compounds (e.g. Beaumont and Maccaferri, 2011) and the potential for residual electrical coupling in Cx gene-deleted mice (De Zeeuw et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the model system, supported by citations.

claim: Preferred frequency and oscillation frequency are not significantly different in mouse TIDA neurons.
source: In mouse TIDA neurons, preferred (0.35 ± 0.03 Hz; n = 15; Figure 6E,F) and oscillation (0.39 ± 0.05 Hz; n = 15) frequencies were not significantly different (Figure 6G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ZAP function experiments.

claim: Mouse TIDA cells set their own pace.
source: and were distributed over a similar spectrum (typically 0.2–0.6 Hz), suggesting that mouse TIDA cells set their own pace.
evidence: This is inferred from the match between preferred and oscillation frequencies.

claim: The preferred frequencies in rat TIDA neurons show a similarly wide range and mean (0.30 ± 0.02 Hz) as their mouse counterparts.
source: Intriguingly, the preferred frequencies in rat TIDA neurons showed a similarly wide range and mean (0.30 ± 0.02 Hz; n = 32; Figure 6B,C) as their mouse counterparts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ZAP function experiments.

claim: Rat oscillation frequencies are clustered within a narrow interval at a significantly lower average value (0.14 ± 0.006 Hz) than preferred frequencies.
source: Yet, the rat oscillation frequencies, as described above, were clustered within a narrow interval at a significantly lower average value (0.14 ± 0.006 Hz; rat oscillation vs. preferred frequency p<0.0001; paired t-test; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing oscillation and preferred frequencies.

claim: Electrical coupling places constraints on the network oscillation frequency emerging from cells with variable preferred frequencies.
source: This observation suggests that electrical coupling places constraints on the network oscillation frequency emerging from cells with variable preferred frequencies.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that rat oscillation frequency is lower than preferred frequency.

claim: Gap junction transmission allows current to flow at higher amplitude at certain frequencies via passive or active filtering.
source: We therefore hypothesized that gap junction transmission, via passive or active filtering mediated through pre- and post-junctional neurites, allows current to flow at higher amplitude at certain frequencies.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed data.

claim: Prejunctional resonance (0.31 ± 0.01 Hz) is higher than postjunctional resonance (0.17 ± 0.02 Hz) in electrically coupled rat TIDA neurons.
source: Using this configuration, prejunctional resonance (0.31 ± 0.01 Hz; Figure 7C) was found to be higher than postjunctional resonance (0.17 ± 0.02 Hz, Figure 7D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from paired ZAP function experiments.

claim: Postjunctional resonance is not significantly different from oscillation frequency (0.13 ± 0.01 Hz) in rat TIDA neurons.
source: which, in turn, was not significantly different from oscillation frequency (0.13 ± 0.01 Hz; p>0.05, Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from paired ZAP function experiments.

claim: Both postjunctional resonance and oscillation frequency are clustered within a narrow interval, in contrast to the broad range of prejunctional resonance frequencies.
source: Notably, both postjunctional resonance and oscillation frequency were clustered within a narrow interval, in contrast to the broad range of prejunctional resonance frequencies (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from paired ZAP function experiments.

claim: Gap junction transmission is implicated in the harmonization of faster cell frequencies to a slow population rhythm.
source: These findings directly implicate gap junction transmission in the harmonization of faster cell frequencies to a slow population rhythm.
evidence: This is concluded from the postjunctional resonance experiments.

claim: Electrically coupled TIDA cells discharge in a stereotyped, highly regular, synchronized slow rhythm.
source: First, we show that rat (electrically coupled) and mouse (electrically uncoupled) TIDA neurons exhibit fundamentally different oscillatory activity: while electrically coupled TIDA cells discharge in a stereotyped, highly regular, synchronized slow rhythm
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: TIDA neurons in the absence of electrical coupling display a range of faster, asynchronous, and less regular frequencies.
source: the same neurons in the absence of electrical coupling, display a range of faster, asynchronous, and less regular frequencies.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Both rat and mouse species harbor a similar range of cellular heterogeneity within the TIDA population.
source: We exploit these differences to show that, while both species harbor a similar range of cellular heterogeneity within the TIDA population (assessed as preferred frequency and membrane properties)
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: The presence of gap junctions imposes a slow, harmonized, narrow frequency band across the TIDA ensemble.
source: the presence of gap junctions imposes a slow, harmonized, narrow frequency band across the ensemble.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: In a gap junction-linked hypothalamic dopamine circuit, the network assumes a harmonized slow rhythm emerging from the preferred resonance frequency imposed by the electrical coupling.
source: Our experimental data show that in a gap junction-linked hypothalamic dopamine circuit, the network assumes a harmonized slow rhythm emerging from the preferred resonance frequency imposed by the electrical coupling.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Early studies of neuronal gap junctions suggested that they operate as low-pass current filters.
source: Early studies of neuronal gap junctions suggested that they operate as low-pass current filters (Furshpan and Potter, 1957).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: As oscillatory current passes between cells through gap junctions, the variable frequencies generated by individual TIDA neurons are restricted and streamlined toward a slow network frequency.
source: As oscillatory current passes between cells through gap junctions – and filtered via the active and passive properties of membranes on either side of the junction – the variable frequencies generated by individual TIDA neurons are restricted and streamlined toward a slow network frequency.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The mechanistic demonstration of the role of gap junctions in current transfer argues against the interpretation that the low frequency is the result of 'network load'.
source: The mechanistic demonstration of the role of gap junctions in current transfer (Figure 7) argues against the interpretation that the low frequency of the rhythm in this system is the result of 'network load' (Hooper and Marder, 1987; Meunier, 1992), the drag imposed upon a connected neural ensemble by its slowest members, whose biophysical constraints may act as a brake on the entire network.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings in the context of previous theoretical work.

claim: The specific frequency emerging out of the electrically coupled network is likely not to be an exclusive product of the biophysical properties of Cx36.
source: The specific frequency emerging out of the electrically coupled network is likely not to be an exclusive product of the biophysical properties of the proteins (in this case Cx36) that form the conducting connexons
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the determinants of network frequency.

claim: There have been several Cx36-linked rhythmically active populations described in the CNS, which oscillate in a wide range of frequencies.
source: there have been several Cx36-linked rhythmically active populations described in the CNS, which oscillate in a wide range of frequencies.
evidence: This is a statement about the diversity of Cx36-linked oscillations in the literature.

claim: Other factors specific to the coupled population may contribute to the specific network frequency.
source: Other factors specific to the coupled population, for example the subcellular distribution of gap junctions, cellular geometry and associated proteins, may be hypothesized to contribute.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential contributing factors.

claim: Two related rodent species have adopted different cellular solutions to the common biological problem of adaptive control of pituitary prolactin secretion.
source: These findings also allow for some observations on biological diversity, by revealing how two related species have adopted different cellular solutions to a common biological problem – the adaptive control of pituitary prolactin secretion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in an evolutionary context.

claim: The two rodent TIDA populations accommodate a similar range of cellular heterogeneity among their intrinsic oscillators.
source: While the two rodent TIDA populations responsible for this control accommodate a similar range of cellular heterogeneity among their intrinsic oscillators, the connectivity that imposes network rules thus differs critically (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: In the rat TIDA network, cellular diversity is accommodated through powerful gap junction connectivity.
source: In the rat TIDA network, cellular diversity is shown to be accommodated through a powerful gap junction connectivity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Cellular diversity within seemingly homogeneous neuronal populations contributes critically to the flexibility and adaptability necessary for survival under variable environmental conditions.
source: Cellular diversity also within seemingly homogeneous neuronal populations has been demonstrated to be not only a core characteristic of how nervous systems are organized, but a feature that contributes critically to the flexibility and adaptability necessary for survival under variable environmental conditions (Manor et al., 1997a; Golowasch et al., 1999; Manor et al., 2000; Prinz et al., 2004; Grashow et al., 2010; see Marder et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The TIDA-prolactin axis is subject to circadian modulation.
source: but it may be speculated that these features are of particular potential benefit in a system tasked with adjusting the animal for recurrent reproductive stages, including pregnancy, and is subject to circadian modulation, as is the case for the TIDA-prolactin axis (Grattan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Diversity within neuronal networks increases flexibility but risks compromising reliable circuit performance.
source: Diversity within neuronal networks, as described here in the TIDA system, presents a trade-off: while it increases flexibility, it also risks compromising reliable circuit performance.
evidence: This is a general principle inferred from the findings.

claim: Connecting intrinsically oscillating neurons together via strong electrical coupling can impose a slow network rhythm that overrides the individual frequencies of cells within the population.
source: We here provide evidence that connecting intrinsically oscillating neurons together via strong electrical coupling can impose a slow network rhythm that overrides the individual frequencies of cells within the population.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: All animal experiments were performed on male animals on postnatal days 21–28.
source: All animal experiments were performed on male animals on postnatal days 21–28
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental subjects.

claim: Experiments had received approval by the local ethical board, Stockholms Norra Djurförsöksetiska Nämnd.
source: had received approval by the local ethical board, Stockholms Norra Djurförsöksetiska Nämnd
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Experiments were performed in accordance with the European Communities Council Directive of November 24, 1986 (86/609/EEC).
source: and were performed in accordance with the European Communities Council Directive of November 24, 1986 (86/609/EEC).
evidence: This is a statement about regulatory compliance.

claim: Recordings were performed at near-physiological temperature (34 ± 1°C) apart from subset of experiments performed in room temperature (24 ± 1°C).
source: Recordings were performed at near-physiological temperature (34 ± 1°C) apart from subset of experiments described in Figure 2 performed in room temperature (24 ± 1°C)
evidence: This is a methodological detail about recording conditions.

claim: The concentration used for TTX was 0.5 μM.
source: The concentration used for TTX (Alomone Labs) was 0.5 μM.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about drug concentration.

claim: Postjunctional resistance between pairs was 80 ± 10 MΩ.
source: Postjunctional resistance between pairs was 80 ± 10 MΩ (n = 10).
evidence: This is experimental data about electrical properties of coupled neurons.

claim: Liquid junction potential was 16.4 mV and not compensated.
source: Liquid junction potential was 16.4 mV and not compensated.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about recording conditions.

claim: Sampling frequency in all electrophysiology data was 10 kHz.
source: Sampling frequency in all electrophysiology data was 10 kHz.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data acquisition.

claim: The TIDA species difference in electrical coupling likely has bearing on species diversity in reproduction and parenting.
source: The evolutionary and physiological implications of this contrariety remain to be explored, but given that TIDA neurons control prolactin secretion (Grattan, 2015), it is likely to have bearing on for example species diversity in reproduction and parenting (Robitaille and Bovet, 1976; Bronson, 1979b; Bronson, 1979a; Limonta et al., 1985; Lonstein and De Vries, 2000; Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the physiological implications, supported by citations.

claim: TIDA neurons control prolactin secretion.
source: given that TIDA neurons control prolactin secretion (Grattan, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Rat TIDA neurons are located in the dorsomedial arcuate nucleus (dmArc).
source: Male rat TIDA cells identified by their location in the dmArc (Figure 1A–B)
evidence: This is anatomical information supported by imaging data.

claim: Mouse TIDA neurons were identified using transgenic dopamine transporter (DAT)-tdTomato-expressing mice.
source: In striking contrast, while age- and sex-matched mouse TIDA neurons (Figure 1D,E), identified by using transgenic dopamine transporter (DAT; encoded by the Slc6a3 gene)-tdTomato–expressing mice (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is a methodological detail about cell identification.

claim: 284 out of 311 mouse TIDA neurons exhibited sub- or supra-threshold phasic firing.
source: also exhibited sub - or supra-threshold phasic firing across different experimental conditions (Figure 1F, n = 284/311; Figure 2B–E)
evidence: This is experimental data about the proportion of active neurons.

claim: Rat and mouse TIDA neurons have no differences in cytoarchitectonic features including somata size, dendritic lengths and branching.
source: Cytoarchitectonic comparison of the TIDA somata size, dendritic lengths and branching (evaluated using Sholl analysis) revealed no differences (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from morphological analysis.

claim: A difference in chemical synaptic or electrical coupling is likely to underlie the two distinct patterns of electrical activity in rat and mouse TIDA neurons.
source: These results indicate that a difference in chemical synaptic or electrical coupling is likely to underlie the two distinct patterns of electrical activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity in intrinsic properties but difference in network behavior.

claim: Connexin 36 (Cx36) is the dominant neuronal gap junction-forming protein.
source: In addition, immunostaining for the dominant neuronal gap junction-forming protein connexin 36 (Cx36; Rash et al., 2000) was performed.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.
